analysis.investment_thesis: Borosil Renewables is India's only domestic solar glass manufacturer — a structurally sound moat — but Chinese import dumping has obliterated margins even as revenue grew, turning a ₹166 Cr profit (FY22) into an ₹87 Cr loss (FY25). At ₹6,987 Cr market cap and 73x P/E on a loss-making business, there is zero margin of safety for a SMILE investor.
key_strengths: Sole domestic solar glass manufacturer — natural monopoly in a structurally growing Indian market
Promoter holding at 58.77% signals skin in the game and alignment
Low D/E of 0.23 and operating CF turned positive at ₹100 Cr in FY25 — balance sheet not broken yet
key_risks: Chinese solar glass dumping is structurally crushing economics: EBITDA collapsed from ₹256 Cr (FY22) to ₹73 Cr (FY25) despite revenue nearly doubling — a fatal margin destruction story
Accelerating net losses: -₹50 Cr (FY24) → -₹87 Cr (FY25); business is consuming equity, not creating it
Market cap of ₹6,987 Cr is 7x Kedia's maximum sweet spot; P/E of 73x on a loss-making company means the market has already priced in years of recovery that may never come
red_flags: Revenue grew 65% (FY23→FY25: ₹891→₹1,476 Cr) but net profit went from +₹71 Cr to -₹87 Cr — textbook case of revenue without profit
Free cash flow negative in 4 of last 5 years; cumulative FCF burn of ~₹900 Cr since FY22
EBITDA margin collapsed from ~40% (FY22) to ~5% (FY25) — pricing power has been systematically destroyed by imports
P/E of 73.3x is meaningless on a loss-making company — overvalued on every realistic metric
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Borosil Renewables has a textbook SMILE-worthy structural position — India's only domestic solar glass manufacturer, riding the renewable energy megatrend, with 58.77% promoter holding and reasonable debt. But the financials tell a devastating story: despite revenue growing from ₹891 Cr to ₹1,476 Cr over FY23-25, operating income stayed flat at ₹58 Cr and net losses accelerated from -₹50 Cr to -₹87 Cr. This is not a growth story; it is a price-war casualty. Chinese solar glass manufacturers, benefiting from massive overcapacity and state subsidies, have flooded Indian markets, compressing gross-to-net economics even as Borosil's topline grows. The company is running harder just to fall further behind.

From a SMILE lens, this stock fails on nearly every criterion that matters. The market cap of ₹6,987 Cr is 7x my upper comfort limit of ₹1,000 Cr — institutional investors already own the narrative. The P/E of 73x on a loss-making business reflects hope, not fundamentals. Finance costs tripled from ₹8 Cr (FY23) to ₹32 Cr (FY25), eroding whatever operating leverage the business should theoretically generate at scale. Until India imposes meaningful and durable anti-dumping duties on Chinese solar glass — a regulatory outcome that has been delayed repeatedly — this company cannot convert its monopoly position into monopoly profits. I would revisit only if market cap falls below ₹1,500 Cr and anti-dumping protection is enacted.
